analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal permitting of construction projects with hard deadlines, less environmental review, and limits on lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The House passed the RAPID Act 233-170 in September 2015, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrote the process agencies follow under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the law requiring environmental studies before major federal projects. It set hard deadlines—two years for a full environmental study, one year for a lighter one—and if an agency missed the deadline to rule on a permit, the permit would automatically be approved and could not be reversed. It let the project's sponsor draft the environmental study itself under agency oversight, capped public comment periods at 30 to 60 days, barred agencies from considering the dollar cost of carbon pollution, and made it harder to sue over a permit by requiring plaintiffs to have commented during the review and to sue within 180 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies seeking federal permits or funding for large construction projects—pipelines, highways, power plants, mines, and similar developments. They get faster, more predictable approvals, automatic approval if an agency misses a deadline, and a much narrower path for opponents to challenge a project in court.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a two-year deadline for completing a full environmental impact statement and a one-year deadline for a lighter environmental assessment, with extensions capped at one year or 180 days.

If a federal agency fails to act on a permit, license, or approval by the deadline, the application is deemed approved, the approval cannot be reversed by the agency, and a court cannot set it aside simply because it happened that way.
Allows the project sponsor—including a private company—to prepare the environmental review document itself, with the lead agency overseeing and approving it.

Requires only one environmental impact statement and one environmental assessment per project, and lets agencies adopt state environmental documents or studies from similar nearby projects less than five years old.
Bars agencies from using the social cost of carbon—the government's estimate of the dollar damage from carbon emissions—in any environmental review or decision.
Limits lawsuits over permits by requiring plaintiffs to have filed a detailed comment during the review and to sue within 180 days of the final notice.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near or use areas affected by federally permitted projects. They get shorter windows to comment, environmental studies drafted by the developer's own consultants, no accounting of carbon damage in the review, and a sharply limited right to challenge a project in court. Agencies also lose leverage: silence becomes approval.

drawbacks.text: A missed deadline means automatic, irreversible approval: a permit application is deemed approved if the agency does not act in time, and the agency may not reverse it and a court may not set it aside for that reason.
The project sponsor can write the environmental study that determines the project's impacts, raising the risk that documents understate harm even with agency oversight.
Agencies cannot weigh the monetized cost of carbon emissions in any environmental review or decision, removing climate damage from the analysis.

Public and agency comment periods are capped at 60 days for draft impact statements and 30 days otherwise, and lawsuits are barred unless the challenger commented during the review and files within 180 days.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill: multi-year NEPA reviews do delay infrastructure, and hard deadlines could speed projects people actually want. The House-passed version also required agencies to analyze effects on employment and on low-income communities and communities of color.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem—federal environmental reviews can drag on for years—but its remedy tilts heavily toward project approval: automatic permits for agency inaction, developer-drafted environmental studies, capped comment periods, a carbon-cost ban, and a narrowed right to sue. The pace comes largely by cutting the safeguards communities use to influence or challenge projects, and the Senate never acted, so the tradeoff was never tested in law.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 233-170 on September 25, 2015, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the next Monday, and the committee never acted before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill on a 15-11 party-line vote in July 2015, and the House debated it under a rule covering two permitting bills in late September 2015.

House Democrats tried to add protections for safe drinking water, air quality near projects, private property rights, and Native American tribes through a motion to recommit; it failed 175-229, with no Republicans in favor.
The bill passed the House 233-170: all 226 voting Republicans in favor, 170 of 188 Democrats opposed, and 7 Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill on September 28, 2015 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where no further action was recorded through the end of the 114th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities near projects and environmental advocates are better off that it died: the existing review process, public comment rights, and ability to sue over permits stayed intact. Project developers gained nothing, and permitting delays continued exactly as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities; the review process stayed unchanged

for.name: Rep. Tom Marino
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the House Judiciary Committee to passage.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill on a 15-11 vote after a subcommittee hearing and markup.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action for the rest of the Congress, leaving it without a vote.

against.name: Rep. Ann Kuster
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add protections for safe drinking water, local air quality, private property rights, and Native American tribes; the motion failed 175-229.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 226 of 246 voting Republicans in favor and 0 opposed, while 170 of 188 Democrats voted no and only 7 crossed over.

industries.industry: Developers and sponsors of large federally permitted construction projects (pipelines, highways, energy facilities, mines)
industries.note: The bill gives project sponsors faster permits, automatic approval when agencies miss deadlines, the option to draft their own environmental studies, and a much narrower path for opponents to sue. The time saved comes largely out of the review and challenge rights of people living near the projects.

industries.industry: Energy and fossil fuel infrastructure companies
industries.note: These companies face the longest NEPA reviews and the most litigation over federal approvals. The deadlines, deemed-approval rule, and ban on counting carbon damage in reviews all directly remove their biggest permitting obstacles.

Agencies lose discretion over timing and can no longer consider comments outside a cooperating agency's stated expertise; a missed deadline converts a pending application into an irreversible approval. The bill treats their caution as delay rather than review.
